title: Animals around us: what they eat, where they live, how they move

summary.text: Ants live in the cracks of our walls, a gecko waits by the tube light, and a crow calls from the window. Every one of these animals has to find food, a safe place to live and a way to move. Humans are animals too. Your child hunts for the animals who share their home, then tests their own teeth on five foods. A mouth fits the food an animal eats, and that is true for a crow, a cow and you.
summary.art: A cut-away drawing of a city flat: ants by a kitchen crack, a gecko by a tube light, a crow on the window grill, a spider in a corner, and a girl eating a carrot at the table.

intro.hook: Who lives in your home? Count everyone. Did you count the ants, the gecko and the spider?
intro.text: Most families count only the people. But many other animals live in a flat too. Ants live in tiny cracks. A gecko hides behind a cupboard in the day. A spider sits in a corner. Each of them eats, finds a home and moves about, just as you do. In this unit we find the animals in our home, and then we find out what our own teeth tell us about what we eat.
intro.art: A girl standing in a kitchen doorway counting on her fingers, with an ant line on the wall, a gecko on the ceiling and a crow at the window.

outcomes: By the end I can name animals who live in or near my home, and I know that humans are animals too.
By the end I can say what some animals around me eat: an ant, a crow, a gecko, a cow and me.
By the end I can say where some animals around me live, and why they choose those places.
By the end I can show how some animals move: walk, hop, fly, crawl, slither and climb.
By the end I can say which teeth I use to bite and which to chew, and why an animal's mouth fits their food.
By the end I can guess, test, count and say what I found.

terms.meaning: An animal is a living being who has to eat food to live. Most animals can move about.
terms.example: An ant, a crow, a cow and you are all animals.
terms.art: A row of an ant, a crow, a cow and a smiling child, all the same size, holding hands and wings.

terms.meaning: Food is what a living being eats to live, grow and move.
terms.example: Rice and dal are food for you. Grass is food for a cow. A moth is food for a gecko.
terms.art: Three plates: rice and dal for a child, a bundle of grass for a cow, and a tiny moth for a gecko.

terms.meaning: An animal's home is the place where they rest, hide and stay safe.
terms.example: Ants make their home in a crack in the wall. A pigeon rests on a window ledge.
terms.art: A wall with a crack and ants going in, and a pigeon sitting on a ledge above.

terms.meaning: Teeth are the hard white parts in your mouth that bite and chew food.
terms.example: Your front teeth bite a piece off a carrot. Your back teeth chew it up.
terms.art: A big friendly drawing of a child's open mouth, with thin front teeth and wide back teeth.

terms.meaning: A beak is a bird's hard mouth. Birds have no teeth, so the beak picks up and breaks the food.
terms.example: A pigeon picks up grains with her short beak.
terms.art: A pigeon picking up rice grains from a balcony floor with her beak.

explanations.definition: An animal is a living being who has to eat food to live. Plants make their own food using light. Animals find their food.
explanations.description: An ant, a crow, a cow and a child are all animals. All of them eat food, breathe air and grow. Most of them move about to find food. Humans are animals as well, one kind among many. Your body has bones, blood and a heart, like a cat's or a cow's. So when you count the animals in your home, count yourself too.
examples: You eat, breathe, grow and move. So does the crow at the window.
A cat, a cow and a human mother all feed their babies milk.
An ant is much smaller than you, but an ant eats, breathes and moves too.
explanations.context: This card says what an animal is, and why you are one.
explanations.art: A child and a cat sitting side by side on a doormat, both eating from a small steel bowl.

explanations.definition: Animals eat many different foods. The shape of an animal's mouth fits the food they eat.
explanations.description: Ants eat sugar, crumbs and dead insects. A gecko eats moths and mosquitoes. A cow eats grass all day. A crow eats almost anything: rice, fruit, insects and scraps. Each mouth fits the food. A cow has wide, flat back teeth to grind tough grass. A gecko has many tiny teeth to grip an insect. A pigeon has a short beak to pick up grains. Humans have thin front teeth to bite, and wide back teeth to chew, because humans eat many kinds of food.
examples: A cow has no front teeth on top, only a hard pad. She grips grass between her bottom teeth and that pad.
A butterfly has a long, thin tube for a mouth. She sips the sweet juice from flowers.
You bite a carrot with your front teeth and chew it with your back teeth.
explanations.context: This card says what animals eat, and how a mouth fits the food.
explanations.art: Four mouths side by side: a cow's flat grinding teeth, a gecko's tiny teeth, a pigeon's short beak and a child's teeth.

explanations.concept: Every animal has a home place
explanations.definition: Animals live where they can find food and stay safe.
explanations.description: An animal's home is near their food, and keeps them safe from danger, rain and heat. Ants live inside cracks in walls and floors, close to the crumbs in our kitchen. A gecko hides behind a cupboard or a photo frame in the day. At night, the gecko comes out near the lights, because insects fly to the light. A pigeon rests on a ledge or on top of an air-conditioner box. A spider makes a web in a quiet corner, where insects fly in. So one flat is home to many animals at once.
examples: Ants live inside a crack near the kitchen, close to the food.
A gecko waits near the tube light at night, where the moths come.
A squirrel makes a nest of grass high up in a tree, away from cats.
explanations.context: This card says where the animals in your home live, and why.
explanations.art: A flat drawn like a doll's house: ants in a kitchen crack, a gecko behind a photo frame, a spider web in a corner, a pigeon on the ledge outside.

explanations.definition: Animals move to find food, to find a home and to get away from danger.
explanations.description: A pigeon walks, nodding her head with each step. A sparrow hops on both feet together. A crow can walk and hop. Ants walk fast on six legs. A gecko climbs straight up a wall. Under each toe the gecko has millions of tiny hairs that cling to the wall. A snake has no legs. A snake bends their body and pushes on the ground with their belly scales. An earthworm stretches long and thin, then squeezes short and fat. Humans walk and run on two legs.
examples: A pigeon walks on the ledge. A sparrow hops.
A gecko runs up the wall and across the ceiling.
You walk on two legs, and a cat walks on four.
explanations.context: This card says how the animals around us move.
explanations.art: A pigeon walking, a sparrow hopping, a gecko climbing a wall and an earthworm stretching, with little arrows showing how each one moves.

explanations.concept: Do the animals around us choose?
explanations.description: A gecko waits by the tube light every night, because moths come there. A crow tries a new food, then comes back for more. An ant tastes a crumb and decides to carry it home. Animals sense, choose and remember. A gecko learns where the moths come, and a crow learns which window has rice. Some scientists use a different word for this. They call it instinct, and say the animal is born knowing what to do.
examples: A gecko comes back to the same tube light every night.
A crow learns which family puts out rice in the morning.
Ants find a sugar spill again the next day.

perspectives.explanation: Animals sense the world, choose what to do and remember what worked. A gecko chose a good place to wait for moths.
Much of what small animals do is instinct. They are born knowing how to do it, and they do it the same way each time.

explanations.context: This card asks if the animals in your home make choices.
explanations.art: A gecko on a wall beside a glowing tube light, looking at a moth, with a small question mark above.

agreed.evidence: Humans eat, breathe and grow like other animals. Our bodies have bones, blood and a heart, like a cat's. Scientists have found that humans and all other animals came from the same ancestors, long ago.

agreed.text: An animal's mouth fits the food they eat.
agreed.evidence: Animals that eat grass, like cows and goats, have wide, flat back teeth for grinding. Animals that hunt, like cats, have sharp, pointed teeth. Birds that crack seeds have short, thick beaks.

agreed.text: Many wild animals live in towns and cities, right next to us.
agreed.evidence: Crows, pigeons, sparrows, squirrels, geckos, ants and spiders live in Indian cities. People who count birds in cities, like the yearly bird counts, find dozens of kinds.

challenging.who: A very common idea, among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: Humans talk, cook, read and build cities. No other animal does all of these.
challenging.against: Humans eat, breathe, grow and have babies, like other animals. Our bodies have the same parts as other mammals. Every animal has their own special skills. A bat finds food with sound, and a human cooks.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: that humans are not animals.

challenging.who: A common belief in many Indian homes
challenging.for: Geckos look strange and move fast, and people fear a gecko falling into food.
challenging.against: The house geckos in Indian homes have no poison. They do not harm people. But throw away food if a gecko falls into the pot. A gecko's body can carry germs, like any animal's.
challenging.context: This card is about a common fear: that the gecko on the wall is poisonous.

challenging.claim: Pigeons and crows are pests and do not belong in cities.
challenging.for: Pigeon droppings make balconies dirty, and breathing in dust from old droppings can make some people ill. Crows sometimes snatch food.
challenging.against: Crows eat scraps and dead animals, which helps keep streets clean. Birds lived in these places before the buildings came. Many families share food with crows every day.
challenging.context: This card is about a real argument: do city birds belong in the city?

big_questions.q: You have front teeth and back teeth. A crow has a beak and no teeth. How does a crow manage to eat so many kinds of food?
big_questions.hint: Watch a crow eat. Does the crow hold the food with a foot? Does the crow break the food into pieces?

big_questions.q: Why does a gecko live in our home, and not in the forest?
big_questions.hint: Think about the lights, the insects that come to them, and the cracks behind the cupboards.

big_questions.q: Our flat is home to people, ants, a gecko and a spider. Whose home is it?
big_questions.hint: Who was here first? Who pays the rent? Who needs the flat?

big_questions.q: If you were a different animal, what would you eat? Would your teeth have to change?
big_questions.hint: Think about a cow's teeth, a gecko's teeth and your own.

story.title: Only Four of Us
story.note: Ponni, Selvan, Amma and Paati are made up. Everything the animals do in the story is true of crows, ants, spiders and house geckos in Indian homes.
text: Ponni lived in a flat in Coimbatore, on the fourth floor. She was six. She lived with Amma, her grandmother Paati, and her little brother Selvan.
One morning, Ponni drew a picture of her family. 'Only four of us live here,' she said.
Amma smiled. 'Are you sure? Look around today, and count again.'

Ponni went to the kitchen first. By the sugar dabba, she saw a thin black line. It was a line of tiny ants. One ant held a white grain of sugar in her jaws. Ponni bent down close. The ants walked fast on their six legs, all the way to a crack under the tiles. Then they went inside, one by one.
'They live in the wall,' said Ponni. 'And they eat our sugar.' She drew the ants on her picture.

After lunch, Paati put a small ball of rice on the window ledge. 'Kaa, kaa,' called Paati. Soon a crow landed on the grill. He held the rice under one foot. He pecked it into pieces with his strong black beak. Then he flew away with a piece of rice, to the tall coconut tree across the road.
'The crow lives in that tree,' said Paati. 'He comes here every day for his rice.' Ponni drew the crow too.

In the evening, Ponni went into the bathroom. High in the corner, there was a fine web. A brown spider sat in the middle, very still. A tiny fly was caught in the web. The spider walked over on long, thin legs.
'Amma! The spider has caught her dinner,' said Ponni. She drew the spider and her web.

That night, the tube light was on in the hall. Moths flew round and round the light. Selvan pointed up and squealed. A gecko was on the wall, right beside the light. The gecko stayed very still. Then, quick as a blink, the gecko ran forward and snapped up a moth.
'Will the gecko bite us?' asked Selvan. 'Is the gecko poisonous?'
'No,' said Amma. 'Our gecko has no poison. The gecko eats the moths and the mosquitoes. In the day, the gecko hides behind the cupboard, where it is dark and safe.'
'How does the gecko walk on the ceiling?' asked Ponni.
'The gecko's toes have millions of tiny hairs,' said Amma. 'They cling to the wall, so the gecko does not fall.'
Ponni drew the gecko next to the light. Then she looked at her picture. There were four people, a crow, a spider, a gecko and so many ants that she could not count them.
At dinner, Paati made dosa, with a carrot salad on the side. Ponni bit a piece of carrot with her front teeth. Crunch. Then she chewed it with her back teeth, round and round.
'Paati,' said Ponni, with her mouth full. 'I bite with my front teeth, like the gecko snaps. And I chew with my back teeth. Which animal chews like me?'
'A cow chews grass all day with her flat back teeth,' said Paati. 'Every animal has a mouth for their own food. The crow has a beak for rice, and you have teeth for dosa and carrots.'
Ponni put down her dosa. She picked up her pencil. In the middle of her picture, she wrote one more word next to her own face. The word was 'animal'.
'Amma,' she said. 'Not only four of us live here. Lots of animals live here. And I am one of them.'
story.epiphany: Ponni finds that her flat is home to many animals, each with their own food, home and way of moving, and that she is one of the animals too.
ask: Which animals did Ponni find in her flat? What did each one eat?
Where does the gecko hide in the day? Why do you think the gecko waits by the light at night?
Why did Ponni write 'animal' next to her own face?
art: A girl drawing her family of four at a table in a small flat, with her mother smiling behind her.
A girl bending down to watch a line of tiny ants carrying sugar into a crack under the kitchen tiles.
A crow on a window grill holding a ball of rice under one foot, with a grandmother watching.
A gecko on a wall beside a glowing tube light, snapping up a moth, while a little boy points up.
The girl's finished drawing: four people, a crow, a spider, a gecko, many ants, and the word 'animal' next to her own face.

games.title: Feed Us! A feeding card game
games.context: This is a card game about what animals eat. Each animal card shows an animal from around our home. Players take food cards and give each food to an animal who eats it.

printables.title: 8 animal cards to cut out and lay in a row

items.b: Eats sugar, crumbs, sweet fruit and dead insects.
Eats almost anything: rice, fruit, insects and scraps.
Eats grains and seeds.
Eats moths, mosquitoes and other small insects.
Eats grass, hay and vegetable peels.
Sips sweet juice called nectar from flowers.
Eats flies and other insects caught in the web.
Eats many foods: rice, dal, fruit, vegetables, milk, and for many families, eggs, fish or meat.
Ant, crow, and you.
Crow, ant, and you. Pigeons peck at rice grains too.
Gecko, spider and crow.
Gecko and spider.
Cow.
Butterfly, who sips the nectar inside.
Spider, gecko and crow.
Pigeon. You eat them too, ground into flour.
Cow, crow and ants.
Ant, crow, and you.
You. A calf drinks milk from her mother.
You, the crow and the ants.
Ants and crows.
You. A crow would gladly take a piece.
Cow and crow.
You, and a crow if you share.

rules: Lay the 8 animal cards in a row, face up. Mix the food cards and put them face down in a pile.
Take turns. Turn over the top food card and read it out with the grown-up.
Put the food card under an animal who eats it. Say how that animal's mouth gets the food.
The grown-up reads the back of the food card. If your animal is on the back, keep the card.
If not, put the card at the bottom of the pile, to try again later.
When the pile is used up, count your cards. Then look at the row. Which animal got the most food cards?

setup.art: Eight animal picture cards laid in a row on the floor, with a pile of food cards beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the animal cards. Pile the food cards face down.

setup.art: A child placing a moth card under the gecko card, while a grown-up reads the back of the card.
setup.caption: 2. Give each food to an animal who eats it, and say why.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 8 animal cards and 16 food cards. 2. Lay the animal cards in a row. 3. Mix the food cards and pile them face down.
flow.say: Every animal here needs food. Your job is to give each food to an animal who eats it.
flow.kid: Look at the animals in the row. Each one needs food.

flow.do: Take turns. Turn a food card, put it under an animal, and read the back aloud.
flow.say: Who eats this food? How does that animal pick it up or chew it?
flow.kid: Turn a card. Who eats this food? Put it under that animal.

ask.q: How does the gecko eat a moth?
good: The gecko snaps the moth up fast.
The gecko grips the moth with tiny teeth.

ask.q: Why does the grass go to the cow?
good: The cow has flat teeth to chew grass.
Cows eat grass all day.

flow.do: At the end, look at the row together. Ask which animal got the most cards, and why.
flow.say: Look at the crow's pile and the butterfly's pile. Why did the crow get so many cards?
flow.kid: Which animal got the most food? Why?

check.why: A cow eats grass and grinds it with wide, flat back teeth. A gecko and a spider eat insects.

games.title: Where Do I Live? A hide-and-seek game
games.players: 1 or more children and a grown-up who hides the cards
games.context: This is a hide-and-seek game about animal homes. A grown-up hides animal cards around the flat, each in a place where that animal really might live. The child finds them and says why the animal lives there.

printables.title: 10 animal cards to cut out and hide

items.b: Hide near a kitchen corner or a crack in the floor. Ants live in cracks, close to crumbs.
Hide behind a photo frame or a cupboard. Geckos hide in dark gaps in the day.
Hide high in a corner. Spiders make webs in quiet corners where insects fly in.
Hide on a window ledge. Pigeons rest on ledges and on air-conditioner boxes.
Hide near a bucket or a plant pot saucer. Mosquitoes lay eggs in still water.
Hide under the kitchen sink. Cockroaches like dark, damp places near food.
Hide near the window that looks out at a tree. Crows build nests high up in trees.
Hide near a light. Many moths fly to lights at night.
Hide near a window with a tree outside. Squirrels make nests of grass high in trees.
Hide on your bed. You live here too!

rules: The grown-up hides the 10 cards around the home, each in a place where that animal might really live.
The child searches the home and finds the cards.
For each card found, the child says why that animal might live there.
The grown-up reads the back of the card.
When all 10 cards are found, the child puts them on a drawing of the home.

setup.art: A grown-up tucking a gecko card behind a photo frame on a wall.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up hides each card where that animal might live.

setup.art: A child holding a spider card found high in a corner, with a grown-up reading the back.
setup.caption: 2. Find the cards and say why each animal lives there.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 10 cards. 2. While your child waits in another room, hide each card where the back says.
flow.say: I have hidden 10 animals in our home. Each one is where that animal might really live.
flow.kid: Ten animals are hiding in your home. Can you find them?
flow.parent: Hide the spider and pigeon cards where your child can reach or see them. Never on a high window ledge outside the grill.

flow.do: Your child searches. For each card found, ask why that animal might live there. Read the back aloud.
flow.say: You found the gecko behind the photo frame. Why might a gecko live there?
flow.kid: Find a card. Why does this animal live there? Say why.

ask.q: Why does a gecko hide behind a photo frame?
good: It is dark and safe there.
The gecko can hide in the day.

ask.q: Why do ants live near the kitchen?
good: The food is there.
They eat our crumbs.

flow.do: Draw a quick plan of your home together. Put each card on the room where it was found.
flow.say: Look at our home. How many animals might live here with us?
flow.kid: Put each card on the drawing of your home. How many animals live here?

check.q: Where does a gecko hide in the day?
options: Behind a cupboard, where it is dark
In the middle of the floor
check.why: A gecko hides in dark, safe gaps in the day, and comes out near the lights at night to catch insects.

experiments.title: The Chewing Test: which teeth do you use for each food?
experiments.context: In this experiment you look at your own teeth in a mirror. Then you eat five small foods, one at a time. For each one, you notice which teeth bite and which teeth chew, and a grown-up counts your chews.
experiments.question: Which teeth do you use to bite and to chew each food? Which food needs the most chews?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which food will need the most chews? Which will need no chewing at all? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every piece is about the size of the top of your thumb. You chew in your usual way, and the grown-up counts every chew the same way. A grown-up does the same test, so we can compare.

materials.item: a small mirror, or the bathroom mirror
a stick of raw carrot or cucumber
a piece of chapati, dosa or bread
a few puffed rice (pori or murmura) or a few cornflakes
paper and a pencil for the tally

experiments.safety: Sit down to eat, and use small pieces. Use only foods your child already eats. A grown-up cuts the carrot.

schedule.what: Look at your teeth. Guess. Test five foods and count the chews. A grown-up does it too.

experiments.record: Draw your mouth, with thin front teeth and wide back teeth. Next to each food, draw a tally of the chews.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results for one child
rows: Front teeth, with a pull of the hand

setup.art: A child smiling wide at a small mirror, looking at thin front teeth and wide back teeth.
setup.caption: 1. Look at your front teeth and back teeth in a mirror.

setup.art: Five small foods on a steel plate: a banana slice, a carrot stick, a piece of chapati, a spoon of curd and a pinch of puffed rice.
setup.caption: 2. Put five small foods on a plate.

setup.art: A child biting a carrot stick with front teeth while a grown-up makes tally marks on paper.
setup.caption: 3. Eat one food at a time. A grown-up counts the chews.

flow.do: 1. Stand at a mirror together. 2. Smile wide. 3. Look at the front teeth, then open wide and look at the back teeth. 4. Touch them gently with a clean finger.
flow.say: Look at your front teeth. Are they thin or wide? Now look right at the back. What shape are those teeth?
flow.kid: Look at your front teeth. Are they thin? Look at your back teeth. Are they wide and bumpy?

ask.q: How are the front teeth and back teeth different?
good: The front ones are thin and flat, like a knife.
The back ones are big and wide and bumpy.

flow.parent: Many six-year-olds have a gap where a milk tooth fell out. That is fine. A bigger tooth is coming. Ask your child to notice if biting is harder there.

flow.do: 1. Cut one thumb-sized piece of each food. 2. Put them on a plate. 3. Ask your child to guess, and to say why.
flow.say: Which food will need the most chews? Which will need none? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. Which food needs the most chews? Which needs none? Why?

good: The carrot is hard, so it needs lots of chews.
Curd is soft, so I can just swallow it.

flow.parent: Write down the guess. Don't say what will happen.

flow.do: 1. Your child eats one food at a time. 2. Before each one, ask which teeth will bite. 3. Count every chew aloud, and make a tally. 4. Ask which teeth did the chewing.
flow.say: Take a bite. Did your front teeth or your back teeth bite it? Now chew, and I will count.
flow.kid: Bite the food. Which teeth bit it? Now chew. Your grown-up counts.

good: My back teeth.
The big ones at the back.

ask.q: Did you need to chew the curd?
good: No, I just swallowed it.
Only a little.

flow.parent: Put a finger on your child's cheek near the back teeth while they chew. They can feel the jaw working. Most children find the curd needs almost no chewing and the carrot needs the most.

flow.do: Now swap. A grown-up eats the same five foods. Your child counts the grown-up's chews.
flow.say: Now it is my turn. You count my chews. Will I need more chews or fewer?
flow.kid: Now count your grown-up's chews. Are they more or fewer than yours?

ask.q: Was the order the same for both of us?
good: Yes, curd was fewest and carrot was most.
You needed fewer chews, but the carrot still needed the most.

flow.parent: A grown-up's chew counts are usually a little different, but the order of the foods is often the same. That shows the food, not only the person, decides the chewing.

flow.do: Look at the tally together. Ask your child to say what they found.
flow.say: What did you find? What did your front teeth do, and what did your back teeth do?
flow.kid: Tell your grown-up what you found. What do front teeth do? What do back teeth do?

ask.q: What do your front teeth do, and what do your back teeth do?
good: Front teeth bite pieces off.
Back teeth chew the food up small.

flow.think: A cow has wide, flat back teeth and eats grass all day. What would a cow's chew count for grass be?

check.q: Which teeth bite a piece off a carrot?
check.why: Thin front teeth bite and cut pieces off. Wide back teeth then chew the piece up small.

activities.title: Who Else Lives in Our Home?
activities.context: In this activity you walk round your home and look for every animal who lives there, and for signs of them, like a web or an ant line. Count yourself too.

schedule.what: Walk round the home. Find animals and signs of animals. Draw them.

activities.record: Draw your home with every animal you found, and yourself.

setup.art: A child shining a torch into a dark corner under a kitchen sink, with a grown-up beside her.
setup.caption: 1. Look in corners, under the sink and by the windows.

setup.art: A child's drawing of a flat with ants, a spider web, a gecko, a pigeon at the window and the child herself.
setup.caption: 2. Draw every animal you found, and yourself.

flow.do: Walk slowly round the home. Look in the kitchen corners, under the sink, by the lights, in high corners and out of the windows. Use the torch for dark places.
flow.say: Let's find every animal who lives in our home. Look for the animals, and for signs, like a web or droppings.
flow.kid: Look for animals in your home. Look in corners and under the sink. Look out of the window too.
flow.parent: Ants, a spider web, a gecko or gecko droppings, a mosquito, a moth or a pigeon on a ledge are the usual finds. Don't touch the animals. Look only.

ask.q: Where did you find the ants? Why do you think they live there?
good: Near the kitchen, because the food is there.
In a crack in the wall.

flow.do: Draw the home together. Put in every animal found. Ask your child who they forgot.
flow.say: Draw everyone who lives here. Did you forget anyone?
flow.kid: Draw every animal you found. Did you forget anyone? Draw yourself too.

ask.q: Did you draw yourself? Why should you?
good: Because I am an animal too.
People are animals.

flow.think: Who lived in this place before our building was built?

activities.title: Gecko by the Light (if a gecko lives with you)
activities.context: If a gecko lives in your home, this activity is a chance to watch the gecko at night by a light. You watch where the gecko waits, what the gecko eats and how the gecko moves.

materials.item: a room with a wall light or a tube light, after dark

schedule.what: After dark, watch the gecko by the light for 10 minutes.

activities.record: Draw the gecko, the light and any insect the gecko caught.

setup.art: A dark room with a tube light on, moths flying round it, and a gecko on the wall nearby.
setup.caption: 1. After dark, switch on the light and wait.

setup.art: A child and a grown-up sitting quietly on a sofa, looking up at a gecko near the light.
setup.caption: 2. Sit still and watch the gecko.

flow.do: After dark, switch on the wall light. Sit quietly where you can see the wall near the light. Watch for the gecko and the insects.
flow.say: Let's sit very still. Where is the gecko waiting? Is the gecko moving or still?
flow.kid: Sit very still. Find the gecko. What is the gecko doing?
flow.parent: Geckos often wait still for a long time, then dash. If no gecko comes tonight, try another night, or look for small black-and-white droppings near the light.

ask.q: Why does the gecko wait near the light?
good: Because the moths come to the light.
To catch insects.

flow.do: Talk about what you saw. Look at how the gecko held on to the wall.
flow.say: How did the gecko move? How do you think the gecko stays on the wall without falling?
flow.kid: How did the gecko move? How does the gecko not fall?

ask.q: How does a gecko climb a wall?
good: With sticky toes.
The toes have tiny hairs that hold on.

flow.think: The gecko chose this light. How did the gecko know the moths would come?

activities.title: Walk or Hop? Watch a bird on the ledge
activities.context: In this activity you watch a bird on a window ledge, a balcony rail or the road. You look at how the bird moves on their feet: walking one foot at a time, or hopping with both feet together.

materials.item: a window or balcony where birds come, or a short walk outside
a few grains of rice to put on the ledge

schedule.what: Put out a few grains of rice. Watch a bird and see if the bird walks or hops.

activities.record: Draw the bird's footprints: one-two-one-two for walking, or pairs side by side for hopping.

setup.art: A few rice grains on a window ledge, and a pigeon walking towards them with one foot forward.
setup.caption: 1. Put a few rice grains on the ledge.

setup.art: Two rows of footprints drawn on paper: one row one-two-one-two, the other row in pairs side by side.
setup.caption: 2. Watch, then draw the footprints.

flow.do: Put a few rice grains on the ledge or the balcony floor. Stand back from the window and wait quietly. Watch how the bird moves.
flow.say: Watch the bird's feet. Does the bird put one foot, then the other? Or both feet together?
flow.kid: Watch the bird's feet. One foot, then the other? Or both feet together?
flow.parent: Pigeons and mynas walk, one foot at a time. Pigeons nod their head with each step. Sparrows hop with both feet together. Crows walk and also hop. If no bird comes, watch on the way to the shop.

ask.q: Did the bird walk or hop?
good: The pigeon walked, one foot then the other.
The sparrow hopped.

flow.do: Now your child tries it. Walk across the room like a pigeon, then hop like a sparrow.
flow.say: Now you try. Walk like the pigeon. Now hop like a sparrow. Which is easier for you?
flow.kid: Walk like a pigeon. Now hop like a sparrow. Which is easier?

ask.q: Which was easier for you, walking or hopping? Why?
good: Walking, because my legs are long.
Hopping makes me tired fast.

projects.title: Animal Puppet Show: eat, live, move
projects.context: In this two-day project you make paper puppets of three animals from your home. Then you put on a show where each puppet says what they eat, where they live and how they move.

materials.item: old cardboard, from a cereal box or a shoebox
3 ice-cream sticks, pencils or straws, and tape

schedule.what: Choose three animals from your home. Draw them on cardboard, cut them out and tape them to sticks.
Put on the puppet show for your family.

projects.record: A photo or a drawing of your three puppets.

setup.art: A child colouring a gecko, an ant and a crow drawn on cardboard, with a grown-up cutting one out.
setup.caption: 1. Draw three animals, cut them out and tape them to sticks.

setup.art: A child behind a table holding up a crow puppet, with a grandmother and a little brother watching.
setup.caption: 2. Put on a show. Each puppet says what they eat, where they live and how they move.

flow.do: 1. Your child chooses three animals from the home hunt. 2. They draw each one on cardboard, about the size of a hand. 3. A grown-up cuts them out. 4. Tape each one to a stick.
flow.say: Which three animals live with us? Let's make a puppet of each one.
flow.kid: Choose three animals from your home. Draw each one. Your grown-up cuts them out.
flow.parent: Good choices are animals your child has really seen: ants, a gecko, a crow, a pigeon or a spider.

flow.wait: Come back tomorrow for the show.
flow.do: Your child holds up each puppet and speaks for that animal. The family asks the puppet questions.
flow.say: Hello, gecko! What do you eat? Where do you live? How do you move?
flow.kid: Hold up a puppet. Talk like that animal. Say what you eat, where you live and how you move.

ask.q: Crow, where do you live, and what do you eat?
good: I live in a nest in a tall tree.
I eat rice, fruit, insects and scraps.

flow.think: If the ant puppet could ask you a question, what would the ant ask?

challenges.title: Invent an Animal Who Could Live in Our Flat
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You invent a new animal who could live in your flat. Your animal needs food they can find there, a safe place to hide and a way to move around.
challenges.problem: Invent an animal who could live in your flat without anyone feeding them. Decide what they eat, where they hide and how they move. Then make them out of dough or paper.
constraints: The food must be something already in a flat, like crumbs, insects or dust.
The animal needs a safe hiding place in the flat.
The animal's mouth must fit their food, and their feet must fit the place they move.
materials: small things for the body, such as rice grains for teeth or matchsticks for legs
general: A gecko eats insects that come to the lights, hides behind cupboards, and climbs walls with clinging toes.
Ants eat crumbs, live in cracks and walk on six legs.
A spider eats insects caught in her web and lives in a quiet corner.
creative: An animal with a long, thin tongue for licking up spilt sugar from inside a dabba.
A flat animal who slides under doors and eats dust and dead skin.
An animal with sucker feet who lives on the bathroom tiles and eats the black mould in the grout.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own flat animal. Give your animal a name. Make them, and tell your family what they eat, where they hide and how they move.

setup.art: A child drawing a made-up animal with long sticky toes and a thin tongue on a sheet of paper.
setup.caption: 1. Draw your animal. Decide their food, their home and how they move.

setup.art: A dough animal with matchstick legs sitting next to a drawing of the flat, with an arrow to a hiding place behind the cupboard.
setup.caption: 2. Make your animal and show where they live.

flow.do: Talk about the animals who already live in the flat. Ask what each one eats, where they hide and how they move.
flow.say: The gecko, the ants and the spider all live here already. How do they manage it?
flow.kid: Think about the gecko and the ants. How do they live in your flat?

flow.do: Your child invents an animal, draws them and makes them from dough or paper.
flow.say: What will your animal eat? Where will they hide? How will they move around?
flow.kid: Invent an animal. What do they eat? Where do they hide? How do they move?

ask.q: Why does your animal have that mouth?
good: Because the mouth fits the food.
The long tongue gets the sugar out.

flow.do: Your child shows the family their animal and tells how the animal lives. The family asks one hard question.
flow.say: Tell us about your animal. What happens to your animal if we sweep up every crumb?
flow.kid: Show your animal. Tell your family about them. Answer their question.
flow.think: Which real animal is most like the one you invented?

items.p: Colour the animals green. Cross out the things that are not animals.
items.why: Crows, ants, geckos and girls are all animals. They eat, breathe and grow. A stone and a spoon were never alive.
items.art: Six small pictures: a crow, an ant, a girl, a stone, a gecko and a steel spoon.

items.p: Draw a line from each animal to the food they eat.
items.why: A cow grinds grass, a gecko snaps up insects, a pigeon picks up grains and a butterfly sips nectar from flowers.
items.art: Four animals on the left and grass, a moth, grains and a flower on the right.

items.p: Draw your mouth, open wide. Colour the front teeth that bite red. Colour the back teeth that chew blue.
items.a: Thin front teeth coloured red, wide back teeth coloured blue.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the front teeth thin and the back teeth wide, as the child saw in the mirror.
items.art: An outline of a wide-open mouth with empty teeth to colour.

items.p: Remember the chewing test? Which food needed almost no chewing?
items.why: Curd is soft, so it needs almost no chewing. Carrot and chapati are tougher, so the back teeth must chew them many times.

items.p: Draw a line from each animal to their home.
pairs: A nest in a tall tree
items.why: Ants live in cracks near food, spiders build webs where insects fly, and crows nest high in trees.
items.art: Three animals and three homes: a wall crack, a corner web and a nest in a tree.

items.p: Humans are animals.
items.why: True. Humans eat, breathe, grow and have babies like other animals. We are one kind of animal among many.

items.p: Write how each animal moves: walk, hop, climb or slither.
items.why: Pigeons walk one foot at a time, sparrows hop with both feet, geckos climb with clinging toes and snakes slither on their belly scales.
items.art: A pigeon, a sparrow, a gecko and a snake, each with an empty line underneath.

items.p: Count the animals in this picture of a kitchen: three ants, a gecko, a girl and a cup.
items.why: Three ants, one gecko and one girl make 5 animals. The cup is not an animal. Did you remember to count the girl?
items.art: A kitchen with three ants by the sugar, a gecko on the wall, a girl at the table and a steel cup.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down: why does a gecko wait by the tube light at night?
items.a: Moths and other insects fly to the light. The gecko waits there to catch them.
items.why: A strong answer links the place (the light) to the food (the insects that come to it).

items.p: Two sisters in Chennai see a gecko on the kitchen wall.

views.says: The gecko should go away. The gecko does not belong in our home.
The gecko can stay. The gecko eats the mosquitoes.

items.ask: Which sister do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other sister has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason, such as 'Nandini, because the gecko eats mosquitoes that bite us.' Then the child is fair to the other side: Kayal is right that we must keep the gecko away from our food.
items.why: Both sisters have a point. The gecko helps by eating insects and has no poison. But any animal walking on food can carry germs, so food is kept covered.

items.p: A cow has wide, flat back teeth. What food are those teeth best for?
items.why: Wide, flat back teeth grind tough grass. Catching moths needs speed and small gripping teeth. Sipping needs a tube.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out? Think about what they eat.
items.why: The gecko, the spider and the crow all eat insects. The cow eats grass and plants.

items.p: Draw a bird's footprints for walking, and a bird's footprints for hopping.
items.a: Walking: one-two-one-two, one foot ahead of the other. Hopping: two footprints side by side, in pairs.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that a walking bird puts one foot ahead, and a hopping bird lands with both feet together.

items.p: Put the chewing test in order.
items: Look at your teeth in a mirror
Guess which food needs the most chews
a: Look at your teeth in a mirror
Guess which food needs the most chews
items.why: First we look, then we guess, then we bite, then we count.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down: a crow has no teeth. How does a crow eat a big ball of rice?
items.a: The crow holds the rice under one foot and pecks it into small pieces with the beak.
items.why: A strong answer says that the beak and the foot do the work that teeth do for us.

items.p: Sort these animals: do they live inside our flat, or outside?
items.why: Ants, geckos and spiders find food and hiding places inside. Cows, squirrels and crows need the street and the trees, but they visit our windows.

items.p: Every animal moves on legs.
items.why: False. A snake moves with no legs, using their body and belly scales. An earthworm stretches and squeezes. A fish swims with fins.

items.p: Here is a picture of a flat. Write where each animal might live: ant, gecko, spider, pigeon.
labels: a crack by the kitchen floor
a high corner of the bathroom
items.why: Each animal lives where they find food and safety: ants near crumbs, the gecko in a dark gap, the spider where insects fly in, the pigeon on a ledge.
items.art: A drawing of a flat with four empty labels: a kitchen floor crack, a photo frame, a bathroom corner and a window ledge.

items.p: Three friends in Pune talk about who owns their building.

views.says: The building belongs to the people. We built it and we pay for it.
The building belongs to everyone who lives in it, the ants and the gecko too.
The birds and the ants were here first, before the building.

items.ask: Who do you agree with most? Why? Then say one thing another friend has right.
items.a: Any side can be argued well. A strong answer gives a reason, such as 'Grace, because the ants and the gecko live here too and need it.' Then it is fair to another friend, such as 'Isha is right that people built it.'
items.why: This is a real question with no single answer. People built the building, other animals live in it too, and many animals lived on this land before.

items.p: Riya, a girl in Class 1, finds a line of ants by the sugar dabba. Where do the ants most likely live?
opts: In a crack in the wall nearby
items.why: Ants live in small cracks in walls and floors, close to food. The fridge is too cold, and the fan keeps spinning.

videos.title: A house gecko catching an insect near a light, slowed down
videos.why: Shows how fast a gecko snaps up a moth, which is hard to see at home.
videos.check: Find a real video of a house gecko (Hemidactylus) hunting at a light. Check nothing is staged or cruel.

videos.title: Close-up of a gecko's toes climbing glass
videos.why: Shows the toe pads that let a gecko climb walls and ceilings.
videos.check: Find a real close-up of gecko toe pads on glass. Check it does not say the toes are sticky with glue.

videos.title: How a cow chews: grass, flat teeth and chewing the cud
videos.why: Shows a cow's flat back teeth grinding grass, to compare with the chewing test.
videos.check: Find a short, accurate video showing a cow chewing. Check it shows that cows have no top front teeth.

quiz.p: Which of these is an animal?
quiz.why: A crow is an animal. A crow eats, breathes, grows and moves. A stone and a chair were never alive.
Humans are animals. We eat, breathe, grow and have babies like other animals.
A gecko eats insects. That is why a gecko waits near a light at night, where insects come.

quiz.p: What does a pigeon mostly eat?
quiz.why: A pigeon picks up grains and seeds with a short beak.

quiz.p: Where do the ants in a kitchen usually live?
opts: In tiny cracks in the walls and floor
quiz.why: Ants live in small cracks, close to the food in the kitchen.

quiz.p: Why does a spider build a web in a corner?
opts: Insects fly there and get caught
Spiders like to look out of the window
The web keeps the spider warm
quiz.why: A spider eats insects. The web catches the insects that fly into that corner.

quiz.p: How does a sparrow move on the ground?
opts: The sparrow hops with both feet together
quiz.why: Sparrows hop with both feet together. Pigeons walk one foot at a time.

quiz.p: How does a gecko climb up a wall?
opts: Tiny hairs on the toes cling to the wall
The gecko jumps from the floor
quiz.why: A gecko's toes have millions of tiny hairs that cling to the wall, so the gecko can climb and even walk on the ceiling.

quiz.p: In the chewing test, which teeth chewed the food up small?
quiz.why: Wide back teeth chew and grind the food. Thin front teeth bite pieces off.

quiz.p: Why did each piece of food in the chewing test have to be the same size?
opts: So the food was the only difference
quiz.why: If one piece were bigger, it might need more chews just because of its size. With the same size, only the kind of food is different.

applications: Doctors and dentists look at teeth to see how a child is growing.
Scientists look at the teeth of a fossil animal to find out what that animal ate long ago.
Families put rice out for crows and water out for birds in summer.
Knowing where mosquitoes lay their eggs helps families stop them breeding in still water.

spotted.text: A crow taking a ball of rice from a window ledge, a sight in many homes across Tamil Nadu and beyond.
spotted.art: A crow on a window ledge with a ball of rice, and a hand putting it out.

spotted.text: A cow on a city street in Varanasi or Madurai, chewing slowly long after she has stopped eating.
spotted.art: A cow sitting on a street corner, chewing, with her eyes half closed.

spotted.text: Pigeons walking and nodding on the steps of a railway station in Kolkata.
spotted.art: A group of pigeons walking on station steps, heads bobbing.

spotted.text: A squirrel running along an electric wire in Bengaluru, tail held high for balance.
spotted.art: An Indian palm squirrel with three stripes running along a wire.

spotted.text: A gecko on the wall beside a street lamp at a tea stall in Guwahati.
spotted.art: A tea stall at night with a lamp, moths around it and a gecko on the wall.

open_questions.q: What does a gecko feel when the gecko catches a moth?
open_questions.why_open: Geckos sense, choose and learn. But nobody knows what being a gecko feels like from the inside.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of animals live in one city flat?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists who search homes carefully find many tiny animals, like mites, that most people never see. Nobody has counted them for most Indian homes.

open_questions.q: Why have house sparrows become rare in some Indian cities?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have several ideas, such as fewer holes in new buildings for nests and fewer insects to feed the chicks. They still argue about which matter most.

ask_kids: Which animal did you see first today? What was the animal doing?
At dinner: which teeth are biting, and which teeth are chewing?
On a walk: is that bird walking or hopping?
Where do you think the ants go when they leave the kitchen?
If a cow came to dinner, which food on the table would she eat?

jokes.j: Why did the gecko sit by the tube light?
jokes.a: For a quick moth-ful of dinner!

jokes.j: What do you call a crow with no teeth?
jokes.a: A crow. Crows never have teeth, silly!

jokes.j: Why do ants never get lost in the kitchen?
jokes.a: They always follow their noses... I mean their antennae!

jokes.j: What did the cow say after a big lunch?
jokes.a: I'll chew on that for a while.

jokes.j: Why did the sparrow never walk to school?
What is a spider's favourite place to learn?
Why did the carrot go to the back of the mouth?
jokes.a: The front teeth sent it there for chewing practice.

jokes.j: What does a pigeon say when she walks?
Knock knock. Who's there? Ant. Ant who?
jokes.a: Ant you going to share your sugar?

maths.problem: In the chewing test, Ponni chewed the carrot 24 times and the banana 6 times. Which food needed more chews? Why do you think so?
maths.explain: 24 is more than 6. The carrot is hard, so the back teeth must grind it many times. The banana is soft.
maths.context: This is about the chewing test, where you counted your chews for each food.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two numbers shows that the hard food needed far more work from the back teeth.

maths.problem: Meera found 3 animals in the kitchen, 2 in the bathroom and 1 at the window. How many animals did she find? Did she count herself?
maths.answer: She found 6 animals. With herself, that makes 7.
maths.explain: 3 and 2 make 5, and 1 more makes 6. Meera is an animal too, so 6 and 1 more is 7.
maths.context: This is about the home hunt, where you looked for every animal in your home.
maths.why_maths: Adding up the animals from each room shows how many share our home, and reminds us to count ourselves.

maths.problem: Divya watched a ledge for a few minutes. She made a tally: pigeons ||||, sparrows ||, crows |. Which bird came most? How many birds came in all?
maths.answer: Pigeons came most, 4 times. 7 birds came in all.
maths.explain: 4 tally marks for pigeons is the most. 4 and 2 and 1 make 7.
maths.context: This is about watching birds on the window ledge to see if they walk or hop.
maths.why_maths: A tally keeps count while the birds come and go, so we can say which bird visits most.

warmup.q: Which teeth bite: front or back?
warmup.a: Front teeth bite. Back teeth chew.

warmup.q: Does a sparrow walk or hop?

warmup.a: In tiny cracks in the walls and floor.
Grass, and she chews it with flat back teeth.

founder: Notebook items bio:16 (Animal Biology) and bio:176 (Animals): headings only, no activities to use.
ideas/by_topic: no notebook page for this topic; habitats-and-adaptation.md and kinds-of-living-things-and-sorting-them.md had nothing at this level.
science: Incisors cut and molars grind in humans; children aged about 6 lose their first milk incisors. Any human anatomy or dentistry textbook.
Cattle have no upper incisors; they have a hard dental pad and grind with broad molars (any veterinary anatomy text).
Gecko adhesion: millions of setae on the toe pads cling by van der Waals forces (Autumn and others, Nature, 2000).
Indian house geckos (Hemidactylus) are not venomous; they feed on insects drawn to lights.
Pigeons walk with head-bobbing; house sparrows hop; crows both walk and hop.
Only female mosquitoes bite, for blood to make eggs; mosquitoes lay eggs in still water.

Mary Anning (1799-1847), Lyme Regis: her observation that 'bezoar stones' lay in ichthyosaur abdomens and held fish bones and scales led William Buckland to name coprolites (1829). Women were not admitted to the Geological Society of London until 1904.
Zhuangzi, chapter 2 (Qiwulun): the passage on people, deer, centipedes, and owls and crows, each liking a different food.
Hypersensitivity pneumonitis from pigeon droppings (bird fancier's lung) is a recognised illness.

roots.context: We have found the animals in our home and tested our own teeth. Now we ask what our mouths tell us about ourselves and the other animals.

deep_truth.truth: In our chewing test, front teeth bit the food and back teeth ground it up. Curd needed almost no chewing, and carrot needed the most. Humans have both kinds of teeth because humans eat many kinds of food. So an animal's mouth shows what that animal eats.
deep_truth.habit: We think of teeth as just for eating, the same in everyone. But every animal's mouth is shaped by their food, so looking in a mouth tells you how that animal lives.
deep_truth.evidence: In the chewing test, thin front teeth bit the carrot and the chapati, and wide back teeth chewed every food except the curd. The hard carrot needed many more chews than the soft banana.

three.who_am_i: You are an animal with teeth for many foods. Your mouth tells the story of what humans eat.
three.what_is_life: Every animal must find food. The ant, the crow, the gecko and you each have a body that fits your own food.
three.what_is_this_world: One flat is home to many animals. Each one lives where they find their food and a safe place.

roots.thread: The ant, the crow, the gecko and you all need food. Each of you gets it in a different way: jaws, a beak, tiny gripping teeth, front and back teeth. One need, food, has given each animal a different mouth. So the animals in one small flat show many answers to the same need.

teachings.source: Zhuangzi, chapter 2 (Discussion on Making All Things Equal)
teachings.teaching: Zhuangzi, a Chinese thinker, wrote that people eat meat and grain, deer eat grass, centipedes like snakes, and owls and crows like mice. Then he asked: which of them knows the right taste?
teachings.link: Our chewing test and our home hunt found the same thing. Each animal eats a different food, and each mouth fits their own food. No one food is right for everyone.

teachings.teaching: To share your food and to care for all living beings is the best of all the teachings.
teachings.link: Every animal in our home needs food, as we do. Many families share a little rice with the crows each day.

science.text: An animal's teeth or beak fit the food they eat. Scientists can tell what a fossil animal ate by looking at their teeth.
Animals sense, choose and remember. What eating feels like to a gecko or an ant, nobody knows.

other_view.view: Many biologists say a gecko waiting by the light is acting on instinct, set off by the light and the moving insects. They say the gecko is born knowing how to hunt, and they would not call it a choice.

practice.title: One slow bite
practice.say: Take one raisin or a small piece of fruit. Close your eyes. Bite it slowly with your front teeth. Feel your tongue move it to the back. Feel your back teeth chew. Before you swallow, think of the crow and the ant, who are eating somewhere too.
practice.kid: Close your eyes. Bite the raisin with your front teeth. Feel your back teeth chew. Think of the crow, eating too.

ask: A crow has no teeth, and you have twenty. Who has the better mouth?
If the ants and the gecko live in our flat too, whose home is it?
Is it fair that some animals eat other animals?
roots.art: A child with eyes closed, slowly biting a raisin, with a crow on the window ledge outside eating rice at the same moment.

how_we_found_out.context: How can people find out what an animal ate, even an animal who lived long ago? This card tells the true story of a woman who found out.
how_we_found_out.story: About 200 years ago, in Lyme Regis, a seaside town in England, a young woman called Mary Anning hunted for fossils. Fossils are the remains of living beings from long ago, turned to stone. Mary's family was poor, and she sold fossils to visitors to earn money. With her brother Joseph, she found one of the first skeletons of an ichthyosaur. Ichthyosaurs were big sea animals with long jaws full of pointed teeth. Pointed teeth are good for gripping slippery fish. On the same beach, people found odd round stones. They called them bezoar stones, and nobody knew what they were. Mary noticed that these stones often lay inside the belly of an ichthyosaur skeleton. When she broke them open, she found tiny fish bones and fish scales inside. The stones were fossil poo! In 1829, the scientist William Buckland named them coprolites. Now people could see what ichthyosaurs ate: fish, just as their teeth suggested. Mary was not allowed to join the Geological Society of London, because she was a woman.
how_we_found_out.who: Mary Anning, an English fossil hunter, with her brother Joseph; William Buckland, who named coprolites
how_we_found_out.when: The ichthyosaur skeleton about 1811 to 1812; coprolites named in 1829
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That the 'bezoar stones' on the beach were just odd stones. Mary Anning found them inside ichthyosaur skeletons, broke them open and found fish bones and scales: they were fossil poo, which showed what ichthyosaurs ate.
how_we_found_out.art: A young woman in a long dress and bonnet on a rocky beach, breaking open a round stone to show tiny fish bones, with a fossil skeleton in the cliff behind her.
